title: Choose Glassbox's visual world
question: The roll dealt Redline. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll. Whichever you pick keeps VS Code-style tabs and panels, both themes, your accent picker, and the keyboard and voice controls.

options.label: Redline
options.lineage: Engineering drawing sheets and redline review markup
options.thesis: Each session is a drawing under review: Claude drafts, you redline, and every change carries a revision mark back to the decision behind it.
materials: cool drafting film (light) and graphite sheet (dark)
0.25mm technical-pen hairlines on a 4px sheet grid
redline ink reserved for what needs you
options.viewport: The session window as one sheet: a title block in the header (repo, branch, ticket, status, cost), the conversation as the drawing field, and a revision table on the right listing decisions and questions, each numbered with a revision triangle that also marks the edit it produced.
options.risk: Hairline drafting can drift into the broadsheet-hairline look if labels go small, tracked and monospace, so labels stay sentence case in the body face.

raised.raise: A change stays marked until you've seen it: new edits, answers and failures keep their redline until you open them.
Everything sits on one measured grid: every size and gap is a multiple of the 4px sheet module, with no exceptions.
Every busy thing says what it's doing right now: agents, services and tests carry a live verb label instead of a spinner.
One state rule everywhere: selected means filled, pressed means inset, disabled means dimmed, across tabs, rows and buttons alike.
One time axis rules the conversation: timestamps sit in a single gutter, so you can scan a long session by time.
One type family does all the work, at five sizes; hierarchy comes from weight and space, not extra faces.

options.label: Gallery
options.lineage: Broadcast control-room galleries: multiview monitors and tally lights
options.thesis: You're the director watching several live feeds: each session is a monitor, and a tally light tells you at a glance which one is on air, which needs you and which is done.
materials: tally lamps: red on air, green ready, amber needs you
options.viewport: Tabs become a strip of small live monitors with tally lamps; the active session fills the main monitor, with a program/preview split between the conversation and the file Claude is editing.
options.risk: The most familiar choice for a monitoring tool, and dark control rooms slide easily into the near-black-with-neon look that reads generated.

options.label: Gate Board
options.lineage: Airport departure boards and segmented boarding passes
options.thesis: Sessions are departures: the board ranks them by who needs you, and a changed row moves in place and stays lit until you've noticed.
materials: tabular figures in a fixed column grid
one alert yellow reserved for changes
options.viewport: A live board of sessions in the tab strip and dashboard, ranked by urgency; the session header is a segmented pass (repo, branch, ticket, model, cost) with torn-edge dividers.
options.case: Fuses well for juggling sessions and wins on clarity of state, but loses on identification: developers don't picture code review as air travel.
options.risk: Uppercase signage type everywhere turns into airport cosplay and costs readability in long conversations.

options.label: Signal Bench
options.lineage: CRT oscilloscope on a signal bench
options.thesis: Claude's work as a live trace on a graticule, triggered and frozen for inspection.
options.viewport: The conversation as a sweeping trace with events plotted against time.
options.case: Fuses poorly: a conversation isn't a waveform, and phosphor green on black is the neon-on-black default.
options.risk: Reads as a hacker theme within a minute.

options.label: Cutaway Town
options.thesis: Every agent visible mid-task in one labelled cutaway scene.
options.viewport: A panoramic scene of agents at work, each building a subsystem.
options.case: Fuses poorly: charming, but wrong register for a tool used for hours at work.
options.kept: Every busy thing says what it's doing.
options.risk: Toy-like; hurts trust in a review tool.

options.label: One-Bit Desktop
options.thesis: Overlapping windows, dither and marching ants as the whole interface.
options.viewport: Sessions as overlapping windows on a dithered desk.
options.case: Fuses poorly: nostalgic, and it breaks the VS Code familiarity you asked to keep.
options.kept: One state rule for selected, pressed and disabled.
options.risk: Retro novelty; no theme or accent support.

options.label: Deep Dive
options.lineage: Technical dive profiles and dive computers
options.thesis: A session as a descent, logged against one depth-time axis.
options.viewport: The timeline as a vertical dive profile.
options.case: Fuses poorly: atmospheric, but no link to reviewing code.
options.kept: One time axis rules the conversation.
options.risk: Mood over task; gradients read decorative.

options.label: Alphabet Storm
options.thesis: Words as matter, transforming as Claude writes.
options.viewport: Streaming text as a moving typographic field.
options.case: Fuses poorly: motion-heavy, and unreadable for long sessions.
options.kept: One type family does all the work.
options.risk: Distracting at exactly the moment you need to read.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean editor-style tool like VS Code or Linear, executed with full craft.
canonCard.viewport: Today's layout proposal: one row of named side tabs, a quiet header and the conversation first.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other developer tool by design.
